content: The evidence regarding the impact of umbilical vein injection (UVI) of uterotonics on other priority outcomes is currently insufficient to recommend its routine use in clinical practice. The expert group emphasized the need for high-quality randomized trials to compare UVI of uterotonics with expectant management in women with retained placenta. These studies should aim to evaluate the intervention's effect on severe postpartum hemorrhage-related morbidity and its potential to reduce the need for manual removal of the placenta. In research settings, UVI of uterotonics may be considered in cases of retained placenta where there is no abnormal bleeding. Retained placenta can be classified into three types, and UVI of oxytocin is likely effective only in cases of placenta adherens, the most common type, which results from inadequate contraction of the retroplacental myometrium. However, existing studies have not distinguished between subtypes of retained placenta prior to treatment, which may have contributed to the observed lack of efficacy in some cases. The dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of recommendations regarding UVI of oxytocin should involve all stakeholders in maternal health care at international, national, and local levels. Efforts should focus on increasing access to maternal health care and strengthening the capacity of health-care facilities to provide high-quality services for all women during childbirth. These recommendations should be integrated into care packages and programs tailored to specific country and facility contexts. The World Health Organization (WHO) will disseminate these recommendations through its regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, and other relevant agencies. The recommendations will also be made available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during scientific conferences and translated into the six official United Nations languages. National and subnational groups may adapt these recommendations to align with existing strategies, which could include revising national guidelines or protocols. Global models, such as those for antenatal and intrapartum care, can be adapted to different countries and contexts to improve the quality of maternal health care. These models aim to achieve optimal physical, emotional, and psychological outcomes for women and their babies, regardless of existing health system policies. The successful implementation of evidence-based policies depends on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes. These processes may involve revising national or local guidelines and protocols, supported by ministries of health, United Nations agencies, professional societies, and other leadership groups. An enabling environment should be created to encourage health-care practitioners to adopt evidence-based practices. In humanitarian emergencies, the adaptation of these recommendations should align with other response strategies and consider the unique needs, values, and preferences of women in such settings. Stakeholders should also develop tools to support the implementation of these recommendations in emergency contexts. UVI of oxytocin is recommended only within the context of rigorous research due to significant uncertainties about its effectiveness. Large-scale implementation should take the form of research designed to address unanswered questions about its efficacy, acceptability, and feasibility. Stakeholders involved in postpartum hemorrhage prevention and treatment programs should be informed of the current lack of sufficient evidence to recommend for or against UVI of oxytocin for retained placenta. Providers and patients should be made aware of these uncertainties. This recommendation does not diminish the importance of high-quality postpartum care to prevent and treat postpartum hemorrhage, including the use of uterotonics, tranexamic acid, intravenous fluids, and blood products. To assess the effectiveness of UVI, rigorous research, such as randomized trials, is necessary. Currently, there is no standardized dilution regimen for oxytocin in UVI, with doses ranging from 10 to 100 international units (IU) and saline volumes from 10 to 30 mL. Injection methods include direct injection into the umbilical vein or using a catheter inserted up to 5 cm from the placental insertion. The catheter method, with an additional 30 mL of saline, has been shown to be more effective in reaching the placental bed than direct injection. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified critical knowledge gaps requiring primary research, including whether UVI of oxytocin is more effective than expectant management or other administration routes in reducing postpartum hemorrhage-related maternal mortality and morbidity. Research should also explore whether UVI is effective for specific types of retained placenta and whether these types can be accurately diagnosed before treatment. Monitoring and evaluation of the recommendation's impact on health outcomes should occur at health service, district, and national levels. Broader efforts to monitor and evaluate maternal and newborn health care quality should continue, using clearly defined criteria and indicators aligned with WHO standards. The recommendation will be reviewed annually by the Executive Guideline Steering Group, which prioritizes new and existing questions for development and updating. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendation may be updated. If no new information is identified, the recommendation may be revalidated. Concerns about the recommendation's validity should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for updates. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates.
